record.original_question: When parking problems on random trees are extended to metric-topology settings, are dimensions 3 and 4 distinguished or critical in an analogous way to the role that these dimensions play in several other probabilistic models?

evidence.quote: Dimensionality issues have remained unaddressed in this line of research and one would be tempted to ask if dimensions 3 and 4 would be special also for this probabilistic problem, similar as they have proven to be in several other cases in probability theory (Hutchcroft, 2025).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the parking process on random trees defined as follows. Let $T$ be a (random) rooted tree. Independently at each vertex $v$, a number $N_v$ of cars arrives, where $(N_v)$ are i.i.d. nonnegative integer-valued random variables with mean $\mu$. Each car attempts to park at its arrival vertex; if that vertex is already occupied, the car drives along the unique path toward the root and parks at the first unoccupied vertex it encounters. If no unoccupied vertex is found before exiting at the root, the car contributes to the outgoing flux $\Phi(T,\mu)$. For natural families of random trees (e.g.\ critical Bienaymé–Galton–Watson trees, random recursive trees, binary trees), the map $\mu \mapsto \mathbb{E}[\Phi]$ exhibits a sharp phase transition at some critical density $\mu_c$.

Now extend this framework to "metric-topology" settings, namely to processes on random metric measure spaces or on continuum random geometries (such as the Brownian continuum random tree, stable trees, or higher-dimensional analogues like random metric measure spaces of a prescribed Hausdorff dimension $d$), where cars arrive according to a Poisson point process of intensity $\mu$ with respect to the mass measure and follow geodesics toward a distinguished root, parking at the first unoccupied infinitesimal location they meet (suitably defined via a discretization-and-limit procedure or via a continuum flow construction).

Question: In this metric/continuum extension, parametrized by an underlying dimension parameter $d$ of the ambient random metric space, are the values $d=3$ and $d=4$ critical or otherwise distinguished — for example, do qualitative features such as the existence of a non-trivial phase transition, the regularity of the flux, the scaling exponents of the critical window, or the geometry of clusters of parked cars change behavior at $d=3$ and/or $d=4$, in analogy with the role these dimensions are known to play in other probabilistic models (e.g.\ percolation, random walks, the Ising model)?
artifact.status_search_result: A recent survey of parking problems on random trees explicitly raises dimensionality in metric-topology extensions as an unaddressed direction, asking whether dimensions 3 and 4 play a distinguished role analogous to other probabilistic models. No work resolving this question was found in the search; the question is posed as an open direction for future research.

status_evidence.title: Short survey of results and open problems for parking problems on random trees
status_evidence.snippet: Dimensionality issues have remained unaddressed in this line of research; one would be tempted to ask if dimensions 3 and 4 would be special also for this probabilistic problem.
status_evidence.claim: The dimensionality question for parking processes in metric-topology settings is posed as an open problem.

status_evidence.title: The phase transition for parking on Galton–Watson trees
status_evidence.snippet: A sharp phase transition is established for parking on critical Bienaymé–Galton–Watson trees.
status_evidence.claim: Phase transitions have been studied on tree models but dimensional criticality in metric extensions has not been addressed.

status_evidence.title: Parking on the Random Recursive Tree
status_evidence.snippet: For random recursive trees, the phase transition appears at density zero and a critical window can be identified.
status_evidence.claim: Existing parking results focus on tree models without a metric-dimension parameter.
